unit: HV (Vickers hardness), mean absolute error on the 104 held-out test rows
tuned_trees_config: GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=600, max_depth=6, learning_rate=0.03, subsample=0.8, random_state=42). It won 3-fold grouped CV on training rows only (CV MAE 73.3 HV, best of 8 configs from 300/600 x depth 3/4/6 x lr 0.03/0.05/0.1) and was scored once on test.
safe_sentence: We tested our small from-scratch neural network on 104 hardness measurements of alloys it never saw during training: its typical miss is about 78 HV, against 177 HV for a guess of the average, and that is about the same as standard gradient-boosted trees (73 HV with default settings, 78 HV after tuning), so it is a rough screening tool, not a precise predictor.
unsafe_sentence: Our neural network beats tree-based machine learning and accurately predicts the hardness of new alloys.
verdict:
The other agent's numbers hold up, and they are modest. I retrained their 5-member ensemble from nn_data.json using their trainer and their chosen settings ([32,16] hidden layers, decay 0.01, 300 epochs, input clip 3, output clamp). It took 3.2 s and gave a test MAE of 78.159 HV, with predictions identical to nn_final.json (maximum difference 0). Naive training mean: 176.8 HV. Their fixed trees: 73.29 HV, so the network loses to them by 4.9 HV on this split. Tuned trees (600 trees, depth 6, lr 0.03, picked by grouped CV): 78.22 HV. That is a tie with the network (difference -0.06 HV, 95% group bootstrap interval -10.4 to +10.1). The network does not meaningfully beat either tree model.

Leak audit, all answered from the code and data:
(a) Input mean and sd, the +-3 clip, the output clamp range and the target mean and sd are all computed from the rows being trained on (inside each fold during CV).
(b) No group id appears in both train and test, and no test input vector is identical to a training row. Allowing for rounding and normalisation (every element fraction within 0.002), no copies slipped past the grouping. The one composition-level match is HfScTiZr against HfTiYZr, which only collide because Sc and Y are both pooled into x_other; their descriptors differ. There are real near neighbours across the split: 4 test rows within 0.005 and 21 within 0.02 in every element fraction (for example Al0.184 vs Al0.179 CoCrFeNi). The split only holds out exact formulas, as the report itself says.
(c) Settings, guards, epochs (fixed at 300, no early stopping) and ensemble members (all 5 kept) come from 3-fold grouped CV on training rows only. The final test is scored once.
(d) The inputs are 37 features: 22 element fractions, 6 processing one-hots and 9 composition descriptors. prepare.py reads only FORMULA and Processing method. No Calculated, microstructure, BCC/FCC, grain size, density, strength or modulus column is used.
(e) The Mlp and seeded functions are byte-identical to /workspace/ncsu-hackathon/src/lib/nn.js lines 5-98 apart from one comment line. There are no trees, no lookup of training labels and no pre-trained weights.

Caveat for the team: with whole alloy systems held out (their CV on training rows), the network's MAE rises to about 102 HV. Repeat measurements of the same alloy and route already disagree by about 37 HV.
